# Research program (generation 1)

## Goal
Find a policy network and training recipe that raise dev success at a fixed training budget. Change only what the task says this search may change (the network, the training recipe, or both); the observation, reward and budget are fixed.

## What earlier searches showed (7 worlds, 84 trials)
- In 6 of 7 worlds every trial scored exactly 0, on dev and in training. That held for about 40 recipes (1 to 4 epochs, 130k to 430k steps, entropy 0.001 to 0.04, gamma 0.9 to 0.99) and many heads: footprint pooling, footprint convolution, per-layer and landing-layer heads, deeper trunks, transformers. Zeros that uniform mean the world differs from its description. Tuning the recipe or adding capacity does not fix that.
- The only success (about 0.22 on both seeds, under two recipes) was a plain conv net with two features. (a) The legal-action mask goes in as input channels under several reshapes onto the grid. (b) Several per-type logit maps are re-laid into the action vector in those same layouts and summed. In the same world, the starting net with the same recipe scored 0.
- Zero-initialised dense remaps, flat MLP heads and per-action attention never learned within budget in any world. A hedge must be cheap and structured, and its matching component must get gradient from the start.
- One world defeated a full hedge over all 8 grid symmetries × 2 index orders, so other kinds of deviation exist.

## The layout-robust net (best known architecture)
Inputs, concatenated as channels:
- obs;
- the mask's placement part reshaped as [T,Y,X] (identity), as [T,X,Y] then transposed, y-flipped and x-flipped;
- 2 coordinate channels.

Body:
- 1x1 conv to 64, then 1x1 conv to 40;
- two residual 3x3 convs at width 40;
- head h = relu(3x3 conv to 32 + 1x1 skip to 32);
- K separate 1x1 convs, each giving T maps.

Map k is laid out in layout k (identity, transpose, flip-y, flip-x), flattened, and the K maps are summed into the placement logits. DONE and value come from a 64-unit ReLU layer over the mean- and max-pooled trunk features. This is about 53k params at r≈1. Recipe: lr 1e-3 to 2e-3, n_envs 128, rollout_len 16, n_minibatches 8 to 16, ppo_epochs 2 to 3, ent_coef 0.002 to 0.01, gamma 0.9 to 0.95, gae_lambda 0.85 to 0.9.

## How to run each round
1. Read every result, including failures. Any nonzero score against 0 is real signal. Differences between nonzero scores smaller than the task's noise figure are ties.
2. Write down what the evidence suggests before proposing anything.
3. **No-signal phase (every trial so far is 0):**
   - Round 1: include the layout-robust net with its recipe. Fill the other slots with candidates that each hedge a *different* possible deviation, chosen from the menu below.
   - Do not spend slots on recipe-only changes, more capacity, or heads that slice channels by their assumed meaning. All of these failed in every zero-score world.
   - Later rounds: cover hedges not yet tried, and build unions of earlier hedges (adding more summed components is cheap).
4. **Hedge menu.** Each item should be a cheap addition to a conv net, with every component live from the start:
   - Action layout: output components under all 8 grid symmetries × type-major / cell-major index order, with the mask fed in under the same reshapes.
   - Anchor or footprint convention: a 3x3 per-type head in place of exact top-left footprint pooling. It also covers swapped 1x2 and 2x1 footprints.
   - Type order: per-type maps mixed by a learned T×T matrix.
   - Channel meaning: a generic learned 1x1 stem over all obs channels, with no slicing by layer or group.
   - DONE: a logit from global features plus the max and mean of the placement logits. A learned per-action bias vector (one value per action, initialised to zero) can also absorb an odd DONE index or action offsets.
   - Obs frame different from the action frame: covered by re-laying the outputs.
5. **Signal phase (some trial scores above 0):**
   - About half the candidates refine the best one with one change each: recipe values within the ranges above, width or depth, or pruning hedge components it does not need.
   - The rest combine it with untried hedges or new ideas about the task's structure: landing layer, build order, when to call DONE.
6. Give every candidate a hypothesis: what changes, why, and what result would refute it.
7. Keep files simple and correct, at r≈1 (cheaper networks are charged r=1 anyway). Trials took 40 to 190 s of the 900 s limit. Per-layer nets, which run the batch times Z, were the slowest.
8. Do not repeat an idea that clearly failed unless you can say what is different this time.

## Revising this program
After each generation of searches, you rewrite this program from the logs of those searches, and the new program is used for new searches, including on worlds of other sizes that you will not see while revising. When revising:
- keep advice that the evidence supports, and say what evidence supports it;
- remove or weaken advice that did not help;
- write lessons that should hold on other grid sizes, not facts that only fit one world;
- remember that a search keeps the starting architecture when nothing beats it, so any reliable nonzero score counts;
- keep the whole program under 1,000 words, including this section.

## How the program is used
The program has two parts.
- The header at the top (the HTML comment that starts with "<!-- header") is read only by the code that runs each search. It sets the number of rounds, the candidates per round and the training seeds per candidate. Bounds: rounds 2-6; candidates_per_round 2-6; seeds_per_candidate 1-3; and rounds x candidates_per_round x seeds_per_candidate must be at most 24. After the search, its selected trial is retrained on 4 new seeds, and that is its score. Keep the header's format and change only its numbers.
- The rest of the program is what each search receives at the start of every round, together with: the task description, the interface rules, the starting architecture, the results so far, and the budget. The searches see scores only.

The policy and its features must be learned. Do not hand-write placement rules or scores, hand-compute features before a learned layer, or hand-set weights.
